rv.q: The finest show of its kind since “Mamma Mia!,” “Moulin Rouge!” is a reminder that jukebox musicals aren’t required to be soulless behemoth tourist traps.
In “Moulin Rouge,” life is beautiful, in a way reality never is.

Baz Luhrmann's playfully postmodern riff on the Hollywood movie musical set in fin de siècle Paris gets amped up for the stage, with Karen Olivo and Aaron Tveit stepping into roles played onscreen by Nicole Kidman and Ewan McGregor.
It’s fun, tuneful and entertaining, and that’s exactly what we need right now.
They'll flock (as they should) to revel in its extraordinary showmanship — some of the best Broadway currently has on offer.

Indeed the production doesn’t just mimic the movie’s hyperactively gaudy style; it dials up the volume exponentially, primarily by updating and supersizing the soundtrack to include selections from a staggering 70 songs.
As pure spectacle, the highly hyped production with ticket prices venturing into “Hamilton” territory is a smash.
And Moulin Rouge! proves that if you go all in on the concept of a jukebox musical—give the people what they want, with maximum gusto and style, and never apologize—it can be addictive as hell.
This is grand date-night pastiche, a unifying communal playlist, an omnisexual dip into a sensual ocean with a few hundred nervous fellow travelers, no worries, being happy, selling tickets.
A Millennial Reboot of Chekhov, and 'Moulin Rouge!' on Broadway. Halley Feiffer translates 'Three Sisters' into Internet-speak, and Baz Luhrmann’s glitzy movie comes into its own onstage.
Yeah, they had us at the lady sword-swallowers.
Your brain recognizes that it had been hearing Whitney all along and you start to realize a bad jukebox musical can, at the very least, make for a good playlist.
What’s left is a propulsive enchantment that, if you fell in love with the film, as I did, still allows you to fall in like with its follow-up.

Any subtext has been shoved into a push-up bra and short shorts. But here, if you insist, are the particulars. Satine (Karen Olivo, ferocious and occasionally tubercular) is the star of a nightclub act at the Moulin Rouge, the 1899 demimonde discotheque owned by Harold Zidler (Danny Burstein, rouged to infinity).
Directed with opulent showmanship by Alex Timbers, this adaptation of Baz Luhrmann's 2001 movie may be costume jewelry, but its shine is dazzling.
That doesn’t mean the show itself is any good—it is, in fact, horrible—but it’s definitely big.
But I don't think I'll be the only one leaning more toward grimace than grin.
Everywhere it should be filthy, it’s scrubbed aggressively clean, yet somehow it’s still a hot mess.
It’s not even very interesting.
And set designer Derek McLane has turned the inside of the Hirschfeld Theatre into a crystal-studded, heart-shaped, hopelessly romantic fantasyland.
With tongue in cheek and heart in hand, not to mention assorted other body parts splitting, contorting and can-canning up a storm, “Moulin Rouge” is a jukebox musical on steroids.
Who needs ecstasy when we've got Moulin Rouge!?

Director Alex Timbers’ production is immersive from the first moment; sword swallowers and kohl-eyed dancers in fishnets prowling the stage like uncaged cats even as the audience still mills before the curtain.
★★★★ "'All You Need Is Love (and Showmanship).' Baz Luhrmann's hit bohemian-Paris movie gets bigger and bolder for Broadway."

Imagine Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance," but as a steamy Spanish tango. Now imagine that's been mashed up with Britney Spears' "Toxic" and The White Stripes' "Army," and vigorously performed by a group of hot-blooded bohemians in early 1900s Paris....
As any Francophile can tell you, red is the signature hue of the new Broadway megamusical “Moulin Rouge,” now at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre.
It’s mostly just an enjoyable night at the theater.

All in all, Moulin Rouge is a high octane rush of a musical, intentionally filled with visual and auditory triggers that are likely to set your synapses ablaze with memories of songs and sights past, as well as the feelings they evoke.
Olivo, who wowed in West Side Story, is miscast in this role.
There are other things to like besides the design in “Moulin Rouge,” but just nothing else that’s quite as thrilling.
Not that the thumping, pumping Moulin Rouge allows you to dwell on its misogyny.

In Timbers’ stage musical, the show collapses under the weight of Logan’s book as soon as any one stops singing and begins regurgitating plot points from “La Traviata,” “Manon Lescaut,” “Adriana Lecouvreur” and “Cabaret.”

As its musical adaptation blazes forth with a whiplash-inducing 70 songs, flashy can-can dancers and bohemian ideals, the fantasy is forced to be grounded in reality and loses some of the film's spectacular spectacular-ness in the process.
A brightly wrapped, intricately decorated package with little inside.

Onstage, “Moulin Rouge!” (directed by Alex Timbers, whose greatest successes have been lower-key, inventive projects like “Peter and the Starcatcher” and “Andrew Jackson”) is clumsy, overcooked and pointless.

This is the best of what a jukebox musical can be: a thrilling burst of color and chorus and nostalgia and bold reimagining. There are a whopping 70 songs you know and love in the show - some full numbers, some just snippets.
Get used to it, because “Moulin Rouge! The Musical” will be a glittering fixture on Broadway for quite a while.

A $28 million toss of the dice from the same folks who gave us the soon-to-depart $36 million King Kong flop, Moulin Rouge is a blithe but masterful merging of Broadway razzle-dazzle and giddy subversion.
I can't recall any show quite as visually over-the-top.

Pandering at every turn and tailor-made for what its creators must assume has become the attention-deficit generation, Moulin Rouge! makes a persuasive case for marking the nadir of Broadway's basest instincts.
It’s a splendid colorful storybook of characters of love and romance, sex and grit displayed in an embarrassment of opulence pitting the idealistic Bohemians against the monied Aristocrats.

cn.t: Critics are dazzled by the spectacular visuals and sensory overload but divided on substance. Most praise Derek McLane's opulent set design and the energetic performances, though some find the 70-song jukebox format excessive and emotionally hollow.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on rows G-L (Tickpick) / D-L (Tickadoo) as the Al Hirschfeld's true center-orchestra sweet spot. This house has an unusually shallow rake for a Broadway musical theatre — Reddit regulars specifically warn 'Orchestra has little to no rake,' so mid-rows behind any head height become a real problem. Rows G-L sit far enough back to minimize Moulin Rouge's set-piece sightline issues (the elephant and catwalk platforms at house left/right) while staying ahead of the mezzanine overhang that drops at row K.

Front orchestra at Hirschfeld is unusual for a Broadway house: the Moulin Rouge runway/Can-Can extension pushes performers well forward and above your eyeline, so front rows require craning and miss the show's upper-balcony stage action. Tickpick flatly says 'not recommend to sit in the first three or four rows,' and Tickadoo notes 'elaborate staging may be partially obscured when the action shifts to the upper levels' — a show-specific warning that wouldn't apply at most houses.

House-left orchestra is the better of the two side orchestras at the Hirschfeld because Moulin Rouge's elephant set piece lives stage-right — obstruction is 'worse on the right,' per multiple regulars. You still lose some far-stage-left action (from the runway and side catwalk), but trade-off is that actors including Christian routinely enter from this aisle. Reviewers repeatedly single out the left side for close actor access ('Jordan Fisher was two feet away,' 'Aaron entered from there at a couple of points').

House-right orchestra has the biggest sightline trade-off at the Hirschfeld but also the biggest actor-proximity payoff for Moulin Rouge specifically. Christian and the Duke both make their debut entrances on this side, and Satine and Nini exit this way — plus the stagedoor lines up with the right-side exits. The cost: the elephant set piece sits stage-right and regulars warn 'on the far right side you'll basically be paying to look at stairs.' Worth it only if you want the actor-traffic side and stagedoor access.

Front-center mezzanine is the specific seat that Moulin Rouge regulars recommend OVER center orchestra — unusual advice for a Broadway musical. The reason is show-specific: the production's scenic design fills the full proscenium top-to-bottom (balconies, ceiling drapes, windmill, elephant), and orchestra viewers 'miss a lot of the theatre's ceiling AND the floor of the stage.' The Hirschfeld mezzanine also juts close to the stage, so A-C feel close rather than distant.

The Hirschfeld mezzanine has an unusual quirk — a walkway between rows F and G — so row G seats have nobody seated directly in front of them. Regulars pitch G as a cheaper alternative to front mezz with effectively the same sightline over rows F. A reviewer who asked about row J 105-107 was told 'that view should be great, you might miss a tiiiny bit of action on the very front of the catwalk but nothing important.'

Mezzanine left is the safer side mezzanine at the Hirschfeld because the elephant — the biggest sightline hazard during Moulin Rouge — lives stage-right. Reviewers from front-A mezz L report 'Jordan Fisher looked directly at my face when the show started' and 'awesome seat, very close to the stage,' but one specifically flagged that 'faces were blurry even though my vision is average' further back, so rear mezz left reads distances more than obstructions.

sg.n: Mezzanine Right (House Right) A-D (front mezz right)
sg.ra: Front mezzanine right is the single most-warned-against section in Moulin Rouge seating threads. The elephant set piece hangs at stage-right and sits directly in your sightline from this angle. 'Avoid mezz right ... unless you like staring at an elephant's trunk.' Multiple repeat viewers confirm the obstruction is specifically show-induced, not a permanent house flaw — worth the callout.

sg.n: Mezzanine Right (House Right) G-H (rear mezz right)
sg.ra: The rear section of Mezz R is the quirky bright spot of this wing: the rear mezz is staggered so that rows in the 'back half' physically stick out further than the row in front, eliminating head-in-front problems. First row of the rear ('eraic' calls it so) also has 'ample leg room here since it's in the first row of the rear which means there won't be anyone blocking a view.' Elephant obstruction flattens out as you move back and up.

Unique to Moulin Rouge at the Hirschfeld: the orchestra pit has been converted into two on-stage table sections flanking a performer catwalk — 5 tables (11 seats) house-left, 4 tables (8 seats) house-right. Performers interact directly with table guests throughout the show. Major caveats that don't apply to any other section: you must be seated 15+ minutes early or you forfeit the seat; no late seating at all in either act 'due to the scenic obstruction and safety'; bench seating at several tables is '2/3 the size of a regular chair' with little padding; children under 12 banned. You cannot see the full set from here and will be turning your head.

vr.q: this was perfect for what I wanted from Moulin Rouge. And I think if you are a Megan Thee Stallion fan, it is impossible not to have fun.
she's not technically the best performer, but she really owns that stage and makes the role her own, and I think fans of hers are going to have a really great time
overall i had a great time it was a lot of fun it's a beautiful show to look at the sets are fantastic especially for a national tour our cast was phenomenal

I think I saw a three star cast perform a five star show... if it's all about having that emotional connection and seeing a really great love story authentically and beautifully portrayed I just don't know if this is the show for you.
